q: Tell me about yourself and your relevant experience.
a:
I'm a delivery leader with 19 years of experience. I know the technology, and I also own the business side.

Today, at NeuSix, I run five programs in AI, digital twins and SaaS. I own everything: pre-sales, budget, clients, delivery and profit.

My career has three parts. First, seven years as a Technical Architect at DQ Entertainment. That's why I can still check an estimate or a design. Second, delivery leadership at Deluxe, Hornbill and Cosmos-Maya. I delivered for Hollywood studios and fixed projects that were slipping. Third, AI and digital work at Brane and NeuSix. I built the Philips X-ray digital twin from zero, and now I run programs for clients in four regions.

Three results I'm proud of. At Deluxe, productivity went up 20%. At Hornbill, delivery got about 30% faster. And on PaySFT, we lost half the team, but still delivered 125 APIs and two mobile apps in 45 days.

So in short: I know the tech, I own the business results, and I have delivered real AI projects. That fits this role well.

Likely follow-up: "Why are you looking for a change?"

I want to lead at a bigger scale. Bigger clients and bigger teams. That's where my experience can help the most.

q: Can you talk about a challenging situation you faced at work and how you overcame it?
a:
My rule is simple. I never risk a client's live system just to hit my own date.

Let me give you an example. At NeuSix, we took over Zolvit, a live AI legal platform. Real customers used it every day. And the people who knew it best were leaving.

Here's what I did. First, we did the handover in steps. We watched them work. Then we ran it while they watched us. Then we signed off. Second, we took full control only when we were ready. We had the guides, the access, the monitoring, and we had practised the common problems. Third, after the switch, we kept support time separate, so new work could not take it away.

The result? There was no break in service. The client's customers didn't even notice.

So for me, a safe handover is better than a fast one.

Likely follow-up: "What would you do differently?"

I would put the handover checks in the contract from day one. Then nobody can push the date before we are ready.

q: Explain a program you built from scratch. How did you establish the vision, success parameters and operating model?
a:
I always build a program in the same order. First the goal. Then how we measure success. Then how we run it.

Let me give you an example. At Brane, I built the Philips X-ray digital twin. It predicts failures in X-ray machines in hospitals. When I started, there was no team, no plan and no target.

Here's what I did. First, I agreed one simple goal: warn the service team early, so they can fix a machine before it breaks. Second, I agreed how to measure success: X days of early warning, and model accuracy above X%. We also worked in three stages, and each stage got money only if the last one worked. Third, I set up one plan for all four teams, with weekly reviews and client demos every two weeks.

The result? The program passed all three stages, and we found problems early, not at the end.

So for me, when the goal is clear on day one, every decision after that is easier.

Likely follow-up: "What if the client can't define success?"

I help them. I ask: which number should change, by how much, and by when? If they still don't know, I suggest a short paid study first.

q: If you joined tomorrow as Senior Delivery Manager, what would your first 100 days look like?
a:
First I listen. Then I fix the urgent things. Then I set the direction. But I don't wait 30 days to act on big problems.

Let me give you an example. At Cosmos-Maya, I had six months to fix several projects. Nobody trusted the status reports, and nobody owned the risks.

Here's what I did. In the first 30 days, I checked every project and made one risk list with a name and a date on every item. By day 60, I gave leadership one report they could trust. By day 90, we were tracking results every week.

The result? On-time milestones went from X% to Y%. And when it's more urgent, I go faster. On PaySFT, I sent the honest status in week one and the new plan in week two.

So for me, have a plan, but don't let the plan slow you down.

Likely follow-up: "What will you NOT do in the first 30 days?"

I won't change things that already work. And I won't promise new dates before I check the facts.

Likely follow-up: "Why should we pay at the top of the band?"

Because better margin and one bigger account are worth much more than my salary. And I have delivered results like that before.

q: How do you establish governance and a delivery operating model?
a:
Governance has one job: to help people make good decisions fast. I keep it simple. Clear owners, a fixed meeting rhythm, and one place for all the facts.

Let me give you an example. At NeuSix, I took over five programs, and each one was run differently. Nobody knew who decided what. And the sponsors got status updates, not decisions.

Here's what I did. First, I made it clear who decides what: the team, me, or the client's steering group. Second, I set a fixed rhythm: daily stand-ups, a weekly review, and a monthly steering meeting. Third, all reports came from one risk list and one dashboard, so nobody argued about numbers.

The result? When PaySFT lost half its team, we acted in week one and still delivered 125 APIs and two apps in 45 days. And at DP World, the steering meetings led to four new projects.

So for me, good governance doesn't slow you down. It speeds up decisions.

Likely follow-up: "How do you stop governance becoming bureaucracy?"

Every meeting must end with a decision, or we cancel it. And we only discuss red and amber items.

Likely follow-up: "What about a project manager who hides red status?"

I make the colour rules clear, so nobody can hide red. I thank people for raising red early. If someone keeps hiding problems, it's a performance issue.

q: A multi-region organisation has inconsistent processes, KPIs and governance. How do you build an operating model that scales but stays flexible?
a:
My rule is: fixed on what, flexible on how. What the client sees is the same everywhere. How each team works is their choice.

Let me give you an example. At NeuSix, we had clients in four regions and four vendors. Green meant different things to different managers, and clients noticed.

Here's what I did. First, I set five standard numbers, with clear rules for red, amber and green. Second, I wrote one playbook together with the leads, based on our best team. Third, I put everything in Jira and Confluence, and let each team pick Scrum or Kanban.

The result? In one quarter, we had one view of all programs. We saw risks two to three weeks earlier, and time spent on reports dropped by about half.

So for me, make what the client sees the same, and let the teams choose how they work.

Likely follow-up: "How do you handle a region that resists?"

I ask what they want to protect. If it really helps their client, I allow it. If it's just habit, I show them the numbers.

Likely follow-up: "How would you know it's working?"

The numbers between regions get closer every quarter, and clients are happier everywhere.

Likely follow-up: "What do you centralise and what do you leave local?"

I keep the standards, tools and quality checks central. Client contact, hiring and daily work stay local.

q: A ₹500+ crore transformation across Cloud, Data, AI, Cyber, ERP and modernisation. How do you build the roadmap, manage dependencies and ensure business outcomes?
a:
I start from the business result and work backwards. I build the basics first: cloud, security and data. And I release money step by step, only when each step works.

To be honest, I haven't run a 500 crore program. But on Philips and DP World, I ran many teams on one plan: cloud, data, IoT, AI and security. The same ideas work at a bigger size.

Here's what I would do. First, link all the work to one business goal. On Philips, everything linked to one goal: less machine downtime. Second, treat data as the biggest risk. In my programs, data causes more delays than AI. Third, make one plan for all teams, so we see the problems where the teams connect.

The result? On Philips, we passed all three stages on one plan. At DP World, we won four new projects.

So for me, big programs fail on the data and on the connections between teams. I plan for both from day one.

Likely follow-up: "Which area would you start with?"

Security and data first, because everything depends on them. AI comes last.

Likely follow-up: "How do you keep business units engaged over several years?"

I deliver something useful every quarter, and each business leader presents their own results.

q: How frequently do you interact with clients, and what meetings do you attend?
a:
I talk to clients every day at team level, and I meet their leaders on a fixed schedule. For me, the client relationship is the main job.

Let me give you an example. At NeuSix, I'm the main contact for the client leaders on five programs, including CEOs. At Brane, I led delivery for Philips.

Here's my rhythm. Every day, team stand-ups. Every week, a program review. Every two weeks, a live demo. Every month, a steering meeting with the client's leaders. And I join every escalation myself.

The result? Client leaders get decisions, not surprises. At DP World, these meetings led to four new projects.

So for me, the client should always hear bad news from me first.

Likely follow-up: "How do you manage clients in different time zones?"

We meet when our time zones overlap, we share the early and late slots, and we send written notes.

q: How do you stay organised and manage your time across multiple programs?
a:
I use a simple system, not my memory. And I spend my own time where the risk is highest.

Let me give you an example. At NeuSix, I run five programs at the same time. Each has a different client, technology and deadline.

Here's what I do. First, every program has the same rhythm: daily, weekly and monthly meetings. Second, one risk list for all five programs. Third, each lead runs their program day to day. I keep three things: clients, big risks, and decisions about money or scope.

The result? When PaySFT got into trouble, I focused on it and we recovered. And Zolvit's live service was never affected.

So for me, when the system is right, I don't need to chase anyone.

Likely follow-up: "How do you decide what to delegate?"

I keep clients, big risks and money decisions. Everything else goes to the leads.

Likely follow-up: "How do you make sure multiple projects are delivered on time, within budget and to quality standards?"

I use the same system on every project, with early warnings for time, money and quality. Quality is built in from the start, with automated tests. When one project slips, I act early, like on PaySFT.

q: How do you balance mature BAU operations with innovation?
a:
The live service comes first. But improvement work gets its own fixed time. Otherwise it never happens.

Let me give you an example. At NeuSix, we ran Zolvit, a live AI legal platform. Support tickets could easily use up all our time.

Here's what I did. First, support work always came first. Second, I split the team's time clearly, and kept about 10% just for improvements. Third, we found improvement ideas in the support work itself, like repeat tickets and manual work.

The result? The service stayed stable, and the client kept getting improvements. Repeat tickets went down by X%.

So for me, improvement needs its own time, even a small amount, or urgent work always wins.

Likely follow-up: "What if the client won't pay for improvement time?"

I show them what the problems already cost them, like repeat tickets. Usually the improvement pays for itself in a few months.

q: Tell me about a program that was in crisis or at risk. How did you stabilize it?
a:
In a crisis, I don't rush to fix things. First I find the real cause. When many projects are red, it's usually one or two shared causes.

Let me give you an example. At Cosmos-Maya, I had six months to fix several projects. Deadlines were missed, nobody owned the risks, and people were moved between projects every day.

Here's what I did. First, I checked every project to find the real cause. Second, I fixed the system: one risk list, one staffing plan, and a clear way to escalate. Third, I showed the teams how one ignored risk had caused a real delay. After that, they owned their risks.

The result? By day 60, leadership had one report they trusted. On-time milestones went from X% to Y%.

So for me, find the shared cause first, then fix it.

Likely follow-up: "What was the hardest part?"

Changing how people think. A process is easy to set up. People only used it after they saw it stop a real problem.

Likely follow-up: "What if you take over a project that is already three months late? How do you recover it without hurting quality or morale?"

First, I take two weeks to understand the real work left. Then I agree a new plan with the client, built on the must-haves. I keep testing in the plan, I clear blockers every day, and I don't make overtime the plan. That's how we recovered PaySFT.

q: How do you manage delivery delays and missed commitments?
a:
Bad news early is a gift. Bad news late is a crisis. When we miss a date, I own it, I make a new plan, and I give the client a clear choice.

Let me give you an example. At NeuSix, on PaySFT, a real estate app, we suddenly lost half the team. We missed dates, and the client escalated.

Here's what I did. First, in week one, I wrote to the client honestly: what went wrong, and what we would change. Second, I made a new plan with only what was really needed for launch. Third, I gave the client a clear option: ₹32 lakh to deliver everything. They could decide with the facts.

The result? We delivered 125 APIs and two mobile apps in 45 days, and the client trusted us again.

So for me, a missed date is a trust problem first, and a schedule problem second.

Likely follow-up: "When do you add more people to a late project?"

Last. First I cut the work to the must-haves and remove blockers. New people slow the team down at first.

Likely follow-up: "How do you know the recovery is real?"

When we hit the new plan two or three weeks in a row, and bugs are not going up.

Likely follow-up: "What if the project is behind schedule but the client still expects delivery on the planned date?"

I tell the client early, with facts and options. On PaySFT, I told them in week one, cut the plan to the must-haves, and gave them a ₹32 lakh option. Clients can accept a new plan. They can't accept a surprise.

q: How do you identify the root cause of a delivery problem?
a:
I find the cause before I fix anything. The data shows me where the problem is. The people tell me why.

Let me give you an example. At Cosmos-Maya, projects were slipping, but nobody knew why.

Here's what I did. First, I looked at the data: goals, money and delivery for every project. Second, I talked to the teams and kept asking why. Why are we late? Because teams are blocked. Why? Because people are shared. Why? Because there is no staffing plan. Third, I checked that this cause explained all the problems.

The result? We fixed the system with one risk list and one staffing plan. By day 60, leadership trusted the reports again.

So for me, when delivery fails, it's usually the system, not the people.

Likely follow-up: "What if the cause is one underperforming person?"

First I check if the system set them up to fail. If not, I talk to them privately, with clear goals and support.

q: How do you manage dependencies across teams and programs?
a:
A dependency with no owner and no date is just a hope. I put every dependency on one plan, and give it an owner.

Let me give you an example. On the Philips digital twin, the AI team needed machine data. That data came from hardware we didn't fully control.

Here's what I did. First, I put all four teams on one plan, so everyone saw every handover. Second, every dependency had an owner and a need-by date, and we checked them every week. Third, we signed a data agreement with Philips, so nobody built on guesses.

The result? We passed all three stages on one plan, and we found problems early.

So for me, plan the handover between teams as a shared goal.

Likely follow-up: "What about a dependency on the client or a third party?"

It goes on the risk list with a date. If it slips, I escalate through the client sponsor, with the cost of the delay.

Likely follow-up: "What if none of those teams, vendors or business units report to you?"

Then I lead with a shared goal and clear agreements, not with authority. Everyone sees the same plan every week. If something slips, I go to that team's manager with the facts. For vendors, it's in the contract.

q: How do you manage conflicting timelines and shared resources across programs?
a:
I protect what can't move. I solve the problem inside the project first. And for real trade-offs, the business decides.

Let me give you an example. At NeuSix, my programs share the same engineers. When PaySFT lost half its team, it needed people. But Zolvit, a live service, still needed its full support team.

Here's what I did. First, I didn't touch Zolvit's support team, because a live service comes first. Second, I re-planned PaySFT for the team it had. Third, I gave the PaySFT client a ₹32 lakh option, instead of quietly taking people from other projects.

The result? PaySFT delivered on time, and Zolvit was never affected.

So for me, priority comes from business value, not from who shouts the loudest.

Likely follow-up: "Two senior stakeholders have conflicting priorities, and both say theirs is business-critical. How do you reach a decision?"

I meet each one first, to understand what they really need. Then I put both options side by side on one page. If they still can't agree, I take it to their common boss, with my recommendation. And we write the decision down.

Likely follow-up: "What if a business leader rejects the scoring?"

Leadership agrees the scoring rule first. Then we only discuss the facts, not the result.

Likely follow-up: "How do you decide what to defer?"

With the same scoring rule, agreed with the sponsors. So it's a business decision, not just mine.

Likely follow-up: "How do you manage resource allocation when multiple projects need the same critical team members?"

I keep one view of everyone's time, protect live services first, and use an agreed rule for the rest. On PaySFT, I didn't move Zolvit's people. I re-planned PaySFT instead. Over time, I train people in more skills, so we don't depend on one person.

q: A critical transformation is near go-live with open risks and gaps. Business leaders want the original date. How do you decide on readiness?
a:
Go-live should not be a fight about opinions. I use a clear checklist, signed by each lead. Then I give leaders options, and they decide.

Let me give you an example. At Jazeera Airport, we built a digital twin of the terminal. The launch date could not move. Two weeks before, live cameras for 2 of 6 zones were blocked by security approvals.

Here's what I did. First, we checked 22 go-live points. So we knew exactly which items were red. Second, I suggested a phased launch: four zones live, and recorded video for the other two. Third, the sponsor accepted the risk in writing, and we practised the launch twice.

The result? We launched on the date with no problems. All zones went live three weeks later.

So for me, don't fight the date. Change what goes live on the date.

Likely follow-up: "What if leadership insists on full scope?"

Then it's their decision. We write down the risk and have a rollback plan ready. I don't block a fair business decision.

Likely follow-up: "What if a red item is a safety or compliance risk?"

Then it's a hard stop. That part does not go live until it's fixed.

q: A client demands faster delivery with the same budget, quality and scope. How do you reach a sustainable outcome?
a:
I don't say yes, and I don't say no. I ask why the date matters. Usually there's an event, and the event doesn't need everything.

Let me give you an example. At NeuSix, the Vigilant client wanted to launch six weeks early for an industry event, with the same budget.

Here's what I did. First, I asked what they needed to show at the event. The answer was two features. Second, we delivered those two features early, fully tested, and the rest on the original date. Third, we reused parts from an old project, and the client agreed to give feedback within 48 hours.

The result? They showed it live at the event and got new sales leads. And we kept our budget and margin.

So for me, "faster for the same money" usually means "I need one thing by one date". Find that thing.

Likely follow-up: "What if they really need everything earlier?"

Then we need more people or more money, and I show how much. I won't cut testing.

q: A strategic client is unhappy because of missed milestones and poor communication. How do you rebuild confidence?
a:
Trust comes back when we keep our promises. I find out what the client really cares about, and I make small promises and keep every one.

Let me give you an example. At DP World, we missed two milestones on a warehouse project. The operations head stopped coming to our meetings. We had been talking to the wrong people.

Here's what I did. First, I met the operations head and asked, "What would help you on Monday morning?" Second, I showed a live demo on their own data every two weeks. Third, every two weeks we made small promises with dates, and we kept every one.

The result? In two months, the operations head was coming to demos and asking for more. Later, we won four new projects.

So for me, the person who pays is not always the person who decides. Find the real user.

Likely follow-up: "What if the client is also at fault?"

I own our part first. Then we keep a shared list of decisions with deadlines, without blaming anyone.

Likely follow-up: "What if the problem is one person on your team?"

I change the person quickly and politely. The client matters more than any one role.

Likely follow-up: "What approach do you follow to manage client expectations and maintain long-term relationships?"

Clear expectations at the start, no surprises, and help beyond the contract. At DP World, this grew into four new projects.

q: How do you measure customer satisfaction and delivery success?
a:
I measure success against goals we agreed at the start. And I check client happiness in three ways: what they say, what they do, and how their leaders engage.

Let me give you an example. On Philips, we agreed success before we started, so the end result was never a matter of opinion.

Here's what I do. First, I agree success up front. Second, I ask about client concerns at every monthly meeting. Third, I watch what clients do. When DP World started sharing new problems with us, that told me they trusted us.

The result? At DP World, trust turned into four new projects.

So for me, success is meeting the agreed goals. Happiness is being trusted with more work.

Likely follow-up: "What if KPIs are green but the client is unhappy?"

Then we are measuring the wrong things. Green outside, red inside. I ask the sponsor what success means now, and change the report.

q: How do you manage long-term clients where informal commitments have developed?
a:
I keep the goodwill, but I make small requests visible. Free favours slowly hurt our margin and tire the team.

Let me give you an example. At DP World, the client got used to sending quick requests on WhatsApp. One Thursday evening, they asked for a new layout by Monday.

Here's what I did. First, I checked the impact on the plan. Second, I gave them options: do it by Monday and move other work, do a small version first, or pay for extra people. They chose, and confirmed in writing. Third, I set up a weekly slot for quick changes.

The result? They still got quick changes, just planned ones. The weekend work stopped, and the relationship grew.

So for me, keep the goodwill, but keep the promises clear.

Likely follow-up: "Won't the client feel you're less flexible?"

No. They still get quick changes, and everything else becomes more reliable.

Likely follow-up: "How do you manage scope changes when a client asks for additional features during an ongoing project?"

I never just say no, and I never do it for free. I check the impact, and give options: swap it, do a smaller version, or a paid change. We did this at DP World, and the relationship got stronger.

q: What business KPIs do you track?
a:
I look at two things. Is our work helping the client's business? And is it good for our business, like margin and growth?

Let me give you an example. At DP World, the same warehouse problems came up in every meeting: space, damaged goods, slow robots and busy conveyors.

Here's what I did. First, I turned those problems into four AI camera projects. Second, each one had an ROI sheet, so we talked about money saved, not technology. Third, we used the client's own numbers to measure success.

The result? Four new projects, a proposal worth X, and a package we could sell to other clients.

So for me, the best business number is delivery that brings the next piece of work.

Likely follow-up: "What margin do you aim for?"

It depends on the contract. I protect it with honest estimates, change control and the right team mix.

q: You are meeting milestones, but profit has dropped because of rework, low utilisation, extra scope and vendor costs. How do you fix it without hurting quality?
a:
Margin problems are often quality problems. I find where the money goes, and fix rework and free work first.

Let me give you an example. At Deluxe, I delivered for Hollywood films like Black Panther. We met every deadline, but costs were 18% over plan.

Here's what I did. First, I measured rework. About 35% of our effort was redoing work. Second, we added our own review before the studio saw anything. Third, we automated repeated steps, combined three vendor plans, and billed every studio change.

The result? Productivity went up 20%, and costs came back to within 5% of plan.

So for me, cutting quality to save money is the most expensive mistake.

Likely follow-up: "What healthy numbers do you aim for?"

About 80 to 85% billable time, less than 5% free work, and less than 10% rework.

Likely follow-up: "Which lever do you pull first?"

Unbilled work, because that's money for work we already did.

Likely follow-up: "How often would you review the bridge?"

Every month for each account, and every quarter for leadership.

Likely follow-up: "What if the project is technically successful but costs are over the approved budget?"

I tell the sponsor early, with a forecast. Then I cut waste and bill the changes. If there's still a gap, they choose: more money, less scope, or more time. That's what I did on PaySFT.

q: What delivery KPIs do you track?
a:
I track six to eight numbers on one page. Some are early warnings, and some are results. If you only track results, you find problems too late.

Let me give you some examples. At Hornbill, I measured delivery time before changing anything. At Deluxe, I tracked speed and rework together. At Discreet Arts, I built a dashboard that turned amber when a team fell behind.

Here's what I track. First, what we promised versus what we delivered. Second, how long work takes. Third, bugs that reach the client, and risks that stay open too long.

The result? At Hornbill, delivery got 30% faster. At Discreet Arts, we saw delays two to three weeks earlier.

So for me, numbers are for making decisions, not for filling reports.

Likely follow-up: "If you could track only one number?"

What we promised versus what we delivered. That's exactly what the client feels.

Likely follow-up: "How do you stop teams gaming the metrics?"

Every speed number has a quality number next to it. And I use numbers to ask questions, not to blame.

Likely follow-up: "Which metrics would you use to predict future outcomes, not just report the past, and how do you turn them into executive decisions?"

Early signs: promises missed, scope growing, risks open too long, bugs going up. I give leaders a range of dates, not one date, and every red sign comes with a decision I need from them.

q: How do you manage risks and escalations?
a:
Every big risk gets an owner, a plan, and a trigger. The trigger tells us when to act. And escalation has time limits.

Let me give you some examples. On Zolvit, we took over only after the handover checks passed. On Vigilant, the AI agents had limits and human approval from day one. On PaySFT, I gave the client a clear ₹32 lakh option early.

Here's how I work. First, one risk list per program, checked every week. Second, escalation in 48 hours to the program manager, five days to me, then to the steering group. Third, I thank people for raising risks early, so nobody hides them.

The result? Zolvit moved with no break in service, and PaySFT delivered in 45 days.

So for me, a risk list says what might happen. A trigger says when to act.

Likely follow-up: "Tell me about a risk you missed."

On Philips, we built on guesses about the machine data, and it didn't match. Now I sign a data agreement on day one (see question 33).

Likely follow-up: "Give me an example of a trigger."

"If the vendor isn't in testing by the 15th, we switch to the backup." It has a date and an owner.

Likely follow-up: "How do you identify and manage delivery risks before they affect project outcomes?"

I watch early signs: dependencies without dates, old risks, missed promises and more bugs. Every big risk has an owner and a trigger.

q: How do you identify and manage vendor and budget risks?
a:
Vendor problems and budget problems usually come together. I use clear owners, the contract, real data, and I raise money problems early.

Let me give you an example. At Deluxe, several vendors worked on the same films, and they often argued about handovers.

Here's what I did. First, every vendor task had an owner, a date and an agreed scope. We settled arguments with the contract. Second, vendors followed the same quality checks as our team. Third, I tracked spend every week, and raised problems early. On PaySFT, I gave the client a ₹32 lakh option instead of hiding the extra cost.

The result? At Deluxe, costs came back within 5% of plan.

So for me, surprises kill budgets. I make money problems visible early.

Likely follow-up: "A strategic vendor misses critical milestones and puts a major product launch at risk. How do you handle the contract, the recovery and the communication?"

I check the contract and send a formal notice. I meet the vendor's leaders and agree a recovery plan with dates. At the same time, I start a backup plan. And the sponsor hears it from me first. The goal is to save the launch, not to win the argument.

q: What is your experience with AI agents or agentic AI?
a:
I have put AI agents into real use. An AI agent is powerful, so it needs controls.

Let me give you an example. At NeuSix, we built AI agents for Vigilant. They research sales leads and write emails for real customers.

Here's what I did. First, each agent could only use a fixed list of tools. Second, a person approved every email before it went out. Third, agents had to pass a test score before going live, and we tracked the cost of every task.

The result? The agents went live safely, and the client showed them at an industry event.

So for me, you don't just switch AI on. You control it.

Likely follow-up: "Explain an AI agent simply."

A normal AI answers questions. An agent takes actions, like sending an email. That's why it needs limits.

q: Have you used tools like GitHub Copilot or Codex in delivery?
a:
Yes. But using it safely was just as important as using it.

Let me give you an example. At NeuSix, our teams wanted to use AI coding tools on client code. So the risk to client data was real.

Here's what I did. First, only approved business tools. Second, no client data in free public tools. Third, a person reviews all AI code, and it goes through the same tests as other code.

The result? The client was happy, and we had zero data problems.

So for me, AI speed only counts if the client can trust it.

Likely follow-up: "What gain did you see?"

[Your real number], measured before and after, as in question 28.

q: How would you measure productivity before and after adopting AI?
a:
I measure speed and quality together, before and after. Faster work with more bugs is not productivity.

Let me give you an example. At Hornbill, I measured first, so I could prove a 30% improvement. At NeuSix, I did the same with AI coding tools.

Here's how. First, measure before any change: delivery time, bugs and rework. Second, compare fairly: similar work and similar teams. Third, always show speed and quality side by side.

The result? At Hornbill, I could prove delivery was about 30% faster.

So for me, if you don't measure before, you can't prove anything after.

Likely follow-up: "What if quality drops?"

We pause and fix the review rules first.

q: How would you encourage AI adoption if the team is resistant?
a:
You can't force people to use AI. You have to win them over.

Let me give you an example. At NeuSix, two senior engineers on [name the program] didn't trust AI code. Others were worried about their jobs.

Here's what I did. First, I listened to each person's worry. Second, I asked the two senior engineers to write the review rules for AI code. So they became owners. Third, we trained on real work, and the team saw me using the tools every day.

The result? [Fill in how many people started using it.]

So for me, people use AI when they see it helps them.

Likely follow-up: "What if someone still refuses?"

I don't force it, but I expect the same results as the rest of the team. Usually they try it after seeing others save time.

q: How would you move a program from a traditional SDLC toward an agentic development lifecycle?
a:
With AI, three things change. Requirements become examples. Testing becomes scoring. And after go-live, we watch it all the time.

Let me give you an example. On Zolvit and Vigilant at NeuSix, normal pass or fail testing didn't work, because AI answers change.

Here's what I did. First, on Zolvit, legal experts wrote real questions with correct answers. Second, on Vigilant, every agent had to pass a test score before release. Third, after go-live, we tracked what the agents did and what they cost.

The result? Agents went live only after passing the score, with accuracy above X%.

So for me, it's a loop: build, test, watch, improve.

Likely follow-up: "What stays the same?"

Code reviews, security checks and release control. We still need good engineering.

q: What do you consider when managing risk in AI delivery, especially in healthcare and finance?
a:
In healthcare or finance, an AI mistake can hurt a patient or someone's money. So I plan for the day the AI is wrong.

Let me give you an example. On Philips, the data came from X-ray machines in hospitals. On Zolvit, the AI gave legal answers to real customers.

Here's what I did. First, data: we removed personal details and moved data securely. Second, accuracy: the model had to meet a target at every stage. Third, people: a person checked the sensitive answers, and experts were involved from the start.

The result? Philips passed all three stages. On Zolvit, [fill in your result].

So for me, with sensitive AI, safety comes before speed.

Likely follow-up: "How do you explain an AI decision to a regulator?"

We record what data the AI used and why it decided. And a person signs off the sensitive decisions.

q: Leadership wants to transform delivery with Jira, Azure DevOps, ServiceNow, Power BI, automation and AI forecasting. How do you design it?
a:
Tools come last. First, I decide what leaders need to know. Then I make everyone work the same way. Then I build the dashboard.

Let me give you an example. At Discreet Arts, leaders only heard about delays on the delivery day. At NeuSix, teams and vendors used different tools.

Here's what I did. First, at Discreet Arts, I built a dashboard that warned us when a team fell behind. Second, at NeuSix, everyone, including vendors, used Jira and Confluence the same way. Third, I try it on one account first, then roll it out.

The result? We saw delays two to three weeks earlier, and time spent on reports dropped by half.

So for me, a dashboard is only as good as the data behind it.

Likely follow-up: "How would you know it worked?"

Forecasts are accurate, managers spend less time on reports, and leaders stop asking for extra slides.

Likely follow-up: "What's the biggest risk in a program like this?"

Messy data. Without clean data, the dashboard looks nice but is wrong.

q: Tell me about a failure. What went wrong, and what did you learn?
a:
On Philips, I made a mistake. I let the team start building before we had the real machine data. When the data came, it didn't match, and we lost time.

Let me tell you what happened. We were under pressure to show progress, and the data wasn't ready. So I let the team build based on guesses. When the real data arrived, it was different, and we slipped by X weeks.

Here's what I did. First, I owned it and told the client early, with a recovery plan. Second, I fixed the cause. We signed a data agreement with Philips on the format and timing. Third, we changed the order of work and won back X of the Y weeks.

The result? The program still passed all three stages.

So for me, the lesson was simple: sign a data agreement on day one. I still do it on every program.

Likely follow-up: "Would you make the same decision again?"

No. Starting early was right. Starting without a data agreement was wrong. Today I would use a signed format and sample data.

q: How do you mentor and develop delivery leads, program managers and architects?
a:
My job is to build leaders, not followers. I give people real responsibility, with support.

Let me give you an example. At Hornbill, my leads were always firefighting, and every decision came to me.

Here's what I did. First, monthly one-to-ones about their growth, not just status. Second, I let them run client meetings while I was there, and gave feedback after. Third, each lead owned a full program. I taught architects to talk about cost, and managers to read the numbers.

The result? The leads ran programs on their own, and delivery got about 30% faster.

So for me, my goal is to be a little less needed every quarter.

Likely follow-up: "A strong performer who is hard to work with?"

I give clear, private feedback on the behaviour. Results matter, but how you get them matters too.

q: How do you manage offshore, onshore and hybrid teams across time zones?
a:
Distance is not the problem. Unclear roles are the problem.

Let me give you an example. At Deluxe, we delivered for US studios from India. At NeuSix, I work with clients in four regions.

Here's what I do. First, clear roles: client-facing people near the client, and most building offshore. Second, a written handover every day between time zones. Third, fair meeting times, and the same tools and rules for everyone.

The result? At Deluxe, we met every studio deadline, and productivity went up 20%.

So for me, it's one team, many places, one standard.

Likely follow-up: "How do you keep remote people engaged?"

Regular one-to-ones, praise in front of the client, and client contact for offshore people too.

q: How do you build compliance (ISO 27001, ISO 27701, SOC 2, GDPR) into delivery?
a:
Compliance is cheap when you build it in from day one. It's expensive when you add it at the end.

Let me give you an example. On Philips, the data came from hospital machines. On Zolvit, the data was legal data.

Here's what I did. First, removing personal data was part of the main plan. Second, people only got the access they needed. Third, security scans ran on every build, and we collected audit proof as we went.

In simple words: ISO 27001 is about security. ISO 27701 adds privacy. SOC 2 shows the controls work over time. And under GDPR, a serious breach must be reported within 72 hours.

So for me, build it in. Don't add it at the end.

Likely follow-up: "First hour of a data breach?"

Stop it spreading, tell our security team and the client straight away, and keep the evidence. Under GDPR, the regulator may need to know within 72 hours.

q: How do you balance DevOps speed with ITIL control?
a:
Speed and control are not opposites. Automation gives you both.

Let me give you an example. Zolvit was a live system that still needed improvements. PaySFT needed fast releases.

Here's what I did. First, small, low-risk changes went through automatic checks. Big changes got a proper review. Second, every change had automatic tests and security scans. Third, after big incidents, we did a no-blame review and fixed the cause.

The result? Zolvit stayed stable, and PaySFT delivered in 45 days.

So for me: Scrum to build, Kanban for support, DevOps to release, and ITIL to run live systems.

Likely follow-up: "When Kanban instead of Scrum?"

Kanban for support work, which is unpredictable. Scrum for planned building.

q: How do you support Sales and Pre-Sales? How do you balance winning a deal with realistic promises?
a:
I help win deals by bringing real delivery facts into the proposal. I would rather lose a deal than win one we can't deliver.

Let me give you an example. At NeuSix, my work starts with pitching and budgeting. At Brane, I proved a solution for WIN Semiconductors before a bigger deal. At DP World, our delivery brought new business.

Here's what I do. First, honest estimates, with the assumptions written down. Second, prove it with a small trial before going big. Third, I own the handover from sales to delivery, so no promise is lost.

The result? WIN Semiconductors' trial worked, and DP World grew into four new projects.

So for me, the best sales tool is a team that keeps its promises.

Likely follow-up: "Sales already promised an unrealistic date?"

I give options, not complaints: what we can deliver by that date, and what the full scope needs. Then we agree it in writing.

q: How would you build a team to shape and deliver a new opportunity?
a:
Two stages, two teams. A small senior team to win the deal. Then a delivery team to build it.

Let me give you an example. At DP World, we shaped four new AI camera projects, and then delivered them.

Here's what I did. First, a small team to shape it: me, two architects and the ROI people. Second, a delivery team with the right skills and a lead for each area. Third, one or two people stayed from the first team to the second, so nothing was lost.

The result? Four projects, each with an ROI sheet, and a proposal worth X.

So for me, small and senior to win it, strong and organised to deliver it.

Likely follow-up: "How do you mix offshore and onshore?"

Client-facing people near the client, most building offshore, and a written handover every day.

q: A customer who has run a business for 15 years asks you to build an application. What would you do?
a:
I wouldn't start with the app. A 15-year-old business already has things that work. I first find the real problem.

Here's what I would do. First, meet the owner and the staff, and see how work happens today. Second, agree one clear goal, like "cut order time by X%". Third, do a short paid study: scope, a simple prototype and a price. Fourth, build in small steps, starting with the biggest pain. And I train the staff and run old and new systems side by side for a while.

This is how I worked with WIN Semiconductors and DP World.

So for me, the owner doesn't want an app. They want their business to run better.

Likely follow-up: "What if they already know exactly what they want?"

I still check it quickly. Most of it is usually right, and the rest is where the real risk is.

q: Walk me through how you respond to an RFP.
a:
I treat an RFP like an early delivery plan. We win by showing we understand the client's problem better than anyone.

Let me give you an example. At NeuSix, I'm part of proposals from the first conversation.

Here's what I do. First, decide if we should bid at all. A fast no is better than a slow loss. Second, ask questions to find the real business need. Third, build the solution with a small senior team, and estimate from real data. Fourth, delivery, finance and legal check it before we send it.

For example, at DP World, we turned problems into four projects, each with an ROI sheet.

So for me, a good proposal reads like the first chapter of a successful project.

Likely follow-up: "What's your win rate?"

Around X%. But I also check the margin of the deals we win. Winning work that loses money is not success.

q: How do you estimate effort and cost for a proposal?
a:
I estimate from facts, not hope. And I write down every assumption.

Here's how I do it. First, break the work into small tasks, estimated by the people who will build them. Second, compare with past projects. On PaySFT, I know what 125 APIs really took. Third, give a range: best, likely and worst. Fourth, add the hidden work, like testing, security and support. Fifth, write down what the client must provide, so changes become change requests.

For example, on PaySFT, I quickly gave the client a ₹32 lakh option, because my numbers came from real data.

So for me, an estimate is only as good as its assumptions.

Likely follow-up: "Sales wants you to cut your estimate to win the deal?"

I show what must change to hit that price: less scope, or doing it in phases. I don't just cut the number.

q: How do you choose the right commercial model: fixed price, time and materials, or outcome-based?
a:
I pick the model based on how clear the scope is.

Here's how. If the scope is clear, fixed price. If it's unclear, time and materials. If it's new, a small fixed-price study first, then the build. Outcome-based only if we can measure the result. And for live systems, a monthly support fee.

For example, with WIN Semiconductors, we did a small trial first, before the big commitment.

So for me, the wrong model can turn a good project into a loss.

Likely follow-up: "The client insists on fixed price for an uncertain AI project?"

I suggest a short fixed-price study first. Then we fix the price for the build.

q: When would you propose a proof of concept, and how do you make sure it converts into a real project?
a:
I suggest a trial only when there's a real unknown. And I agree success and the next step before we start.

Let me give you an example. At Brane, I ran a trial for WIN Semiconductors and proved it worked.

Here's how. First, the trial answers one big question. Second, it has a fixed time and team. Third, we agree in writing what success looks like, and what happens if it works. And if possible, the client pays something.

The result? It worked, and we proved it.

So for me, a trial with no agreed next step is just free work.

Likely follow-up: "The client wants the POC for free?"

For an important client, I may invest some effort. But I still agree success and the next step.

q: How do you differentiate your proposal against competitors?
a:
Others can match our price and technology. They can't match a team that understands the client's business and has done it before.

Here's what I do. First, start with the client's problem and numbers. Second, show real results, like 125 APIs in 45 days on PaySFT. Third, show how we'll manage the risk. Fourth, bring the real delivery team. Fifth, show a working demo. On Philips, a live demo built trust fast.

For example, at DP World, our ROI sheets meant we talked about business value, not technology.

So for me, clients buy the team they trust.

Likely follow-up: "What if a competitor is much cheaper?"

I show the full cost, including risk and delays. I may offer a smaller first phase. I don't cut quality to win.

q: How do you manage delivery risk in the contract?
a:
A bad deal costs more than a lost deal. So the contract must match the real risk.

Here's what I do. First, write the assumptions in the contract: scope, what the client gives, and what's not included. Second, a clear process for changes. Third, clear rules for when work is done. Fourth, fair penalties, checked with legal.

For example, on PaySFT, having a clear priced option ready protected our margin and the client's trust.

So for me, the cheapest time to fix a risk is before you sign.

q: How do you manage the handover from sales to delivery?
a:
Nothing promised in the sale should be lost in delivery.

Here's what I do. First, the delivery lead joins before the proposal goes out. Second, a written handover pack with scope, promises and risks. Third, one kick-off meeting with sales, delivery and the client together. And the account manager stays in the monthly meetings.

For example, at DP World, the people who shaped the deal stayed on to deliver it.

So for me, most delivery problems start with a promise nobody wrote down.

Likely follow-up: "Sales made a promise that delivery can't keep?"

I raise it straight away, with options, and we agree a written change.

q: How do you grow an existing account through delivery?
a:
The best way to grow an account is to solve the client's next problem.

Here's how. First, deliver well. Trust comes first. Second, listen for new problems in every meeting. Third, turn them into short proposals with ROI. And I share ideas with the account manager every quarter.

For example, at DP World, I turned repeated problems into four AI projects, and the account grew.

So for me, growing an account is not selling. It's solving the next problem.

Likely follow-up: "How do you avoid sounding like a salesperson?"

I only suggest things linked to a problem the client raised. If it doesn't help them, I don't suggest it.

q: How is pre-sales different for AI projects?
a:
With AI, nobody knows the accuracy until we see the client's data. So I sell a way to prove it, not a promise.

Here's how. First, start with the business value. Second, check the data early. Third, do a paid trial on real data first. Fourth, agree the test and the target score. Fifth, show the running cost and the safety controls.

For example, on Vigilant, agents went live only after passing the agreed score.

So for me, never promise AI accuracy before you see the data.

Likely follow-up: "The client expects 100% accuracy?"

No AI is 100% accurate. We agree what is good enough, and add a human check where it matters.

q: What parameters do you consider for an RFP?
a:
Before we bid, I check eight things. Can we win it? Can we deliver it? Can we make money?

The eight things are: the client's real problem, our relationship with them, how clear the scope is, the budget and margin, whether we have the people, the contract risks, the competition, and the strategic value.

If several are weak, we walk away. A fast no is better than a slow loss.

For example, at DP World, focusing on the real problem gave us four projects. And on PaySFT, real data let me give a clear ₹32 lakh option.

So for me, the question is not just "can we win?" It's "can we deliver it well?"

Likely follow-up: "Which parameter matters most?"

Delivery risk. We can talk about price. But if we can't deliver, we lose the margin and the client.

Likely follow-up: "Tell me about a deal you walked away from."

[Name the deal and why you walked away.] I'd rather explain why we didn't bid than why we lost money.

q: Tell me about a deal or proposal you helped win.
a:
The deal I'm proudest of was won by solving a problem the client had already told us about.

Let me give you an example. At DP World, the same warehouse problems came up in every meeting.

Here's what I did. First, I picked the problems costing them the most. Second, a small team turned them into four AI camera projects, each with an ROI sheet. Third, we suggested starting with one, to prove the value.

The result? A proposal worth X, the first project approved, and the account grew into four projects.

So for me, the easiest deal to win is with a client who already trusts you.

Likely follow-up: "What did you learn from a deal you lost?"

On [name the deal], we lost because [fill in the reason]. Now I always start with the client's problem and bring the delivery team.

q: How do you prepare for a client presentation, orals or a solution demo?
a:
Clients buy the team, not the slides. So I prepare a clear story, the real team, and a working demo.

Let me give you an example. On Philips, leaders saw a working digital twin, not slides, and that built trust fast.

Here's how I prepare. First, I learn what each person cares about: cost, risk or results. Second, one simple story: their problem, our solution, our proof. Third, the delivery team presents their part. Fourth, a live demo. And we practise the hard questions twice.

The result? On Philips and with WIN Semiconductors, the demo built trust.

So for me, the pitch should feel like a project that's already going well.

Likely follow-up: "What if you get a question you can't answer?"

I say so, and promise a written answer by a set time. Guessing costs more than a short pause.

q: How do you price a deal and protect the margin?
a:
I start with what the work really costs. Then I set the price.

Let me give you an example. At NeuSix, I build the cost model myself. On PaySFT, I quickly gave a ₹32 lakh option because the numbers were real.

Here's how. First, turn the estimate into a team plan. Second, use the right mix: senior people near the client, most building offshore. Third, add hidden costs, like tools, cloud and support. Fourth, check the margin is X%. If not, change the scope or phases, not just the number.

The result? Sales can see exactly where the margin comes from.

So for me, a deal that loses money is not a win.

Likely follow-up: "Would you ever accept a lower margin?"

Yes, for a strategic win. But leadership approves it, and we have a plan to recover it later.

q: The client asks for a big discount just before signing. How do you respond?
a:
I never give a discount for nothing. If the price goes down, something else must change.

Let me give you an example of the same idea. On Vigilant, the client wanted an early launch with the same budget (see question 17). We found what they really needed, cut the scope, and they gave faster feedback in return.

Here's what I do. First, ask why they want a discount. Second, offer trades: a smaller first phase, a longer timeline, or a longer contract. Third, know my lowest margin before the meeting. And update the contract to match.

The result? The client gets a price they can afford, and we don't do everything for less.

So for me, a discount with no change in scope is just a planned loss.

Likely follow-up: "What if Sales has already agreed the discount?"

I show the impact on margin and risk, and suggest what we change. We fix it before signing.

q: How do you build a business case or ROI for a client?
a:
I write the business case in the client's numbers: what the problem costs today, and when they get their money back.

Let me give you an example. At DP World, each of the four projects had its own ROI sheet.

Here's how. First, measure what the problem costs now. Second, estimate the savings carefully, as a range. Third, show the full cost, including running costs. Fourth, show the payback time, like X months. And agree how we'll measure it after go-live.

The result? The DP World account grew into four projects.

So for me, leaders approve a business case, not technology.

Likely follow-up: "What if the client won't share their numbers?"

I use industry numbers as a starting point, and suggest a short study to get their real numbers.

q: How do you plan transition and knowledge transfer in a proposal when taking over from another vendor?
a:
Taking over from another vendor is risky. So I plan it, price it, and only take over when we're ready.

Let me give you an example. At NeuSix, we took over Zolvit, a live legal platform, from the team that built it (see question 2).

Here's what I do. First, check what we're taking over: code, documents and open issues. Second, a step-by-step plan: watch them, then run it with them watching, then sign off. Third, put the handover checks in the contract, and price the handover separately.

The result? Zolvit moved over with no break in service.

So for me, a safe handover is better than a fast one.

Likely follow-up: "What if the outgoing vendor doesn't cooperate?"

I raise it with the client, because they control that contract. Meanwhile, we learn from the code, tickets and users.

q: How do you handle an RFP with unclear requirements or a very tight deadline?
a:
I don't guess quietly. I ask questions early and write down every assumption.

Let me give you an example. On [name the proposal], we had X days, and [fill in what was unclear].

Here's what I do. First, decide fast if we should bid. Second, send questions to the client early. Third, list every assumption in the proposal. Fourth, plan backwards from the deadline, with one owner per section. If the scope is too unclear, I suggest a paid study first.

The result? We submit on time, and the client sees what the price is based on.

So for me, unclear needs are a reason to write assumptions, not to guess.

Likely follow-up: "What if the client won't answer the clarification questions?"

Then the assumptions become part of the price. If one is wrong, it becomes a change request.

q: You inherit a global delivery portfolio with multiple strategic programmes, but 30% are already showing schedule pressure, resource constraints and escalating client concerns. The executive team expects delivery to remain stable without significant additional headcount. How would you regain control of the portfolio and establish predictable delivery?
a:
Three steps: get the facts, set priorities, and set a rhythm. Usually we don't need more people. The people are just spread too thin.

Let me give you an example. At Cosmos-Maya, projects were slipping, clients were unhappy, and there was no budget to hire.

Here's what I did. First, I checked the real status of every project. Second, I put my best leads on the most important projects. Third, one staffing plan, a weekly review, and a rule to decide within 48 hours. And I stopped low-value work to free up people.

The result? By day 60, leadership had one report they trusted.

So for me, fewer priorities done well beats more people.

Likely follow-up: "How would you explain the planned slip to that client?"

Early, in person, with a new date I'm sure about.

Likely follow-up: "What decision would you most likely ask executives for?"

Usually to stop or delay low-value work. That frees people fastest.

q: A high-value client threatens to terminate a strategic engagement after repeated delivery issues, while the delivery organisation believes the problems are primarily caused by changing client requirements and delayed decisions. How would you stabilise the relationship, protect commercial value and restore delivery credibility?
a:
Usually both sides are partly right. So I replace blame with facts.

Let me give you an example. At DP World, the client was unhappy, and we had been working with the wrong people.

Here's what I would do. First, meet the client leader fast and own our part first. Second, bring facts from both sides, like the number of changes and late decisions. Third, agree a simple change process and a decision list. Fourth, make small promises and keep them, with a quick win in 30 days.

The result? At DP World, trust came back, and we won four new projects.

So for me, own your part first. Then the facts do the rest.

Likely follow-up: "What if the client refuses a change-control process?"

I explain it protects their budget. I start small, with a weekly decision list.

Likely follow-up: "What if they still terminate?"

Then I make the exit professional, with a clean handover. How you leave decides if they call you back.

q: You inherit a delivery organisation with inconsistent processes, low productivity, recurring escalations and weak governance. How would you transform the delivery model and demonstrate measurable improvements within the first year?
a:
I do it in four steps, one per quarter: stabilise, standardise, improve, and make it last. And I measure everything from day 30.

Let me give you an example. I did turnarounds like this at Hornbill and Cosmos-Maya.

Here's the plan. Quarter one: measure and fix the top problems. Quarter two: one playbook and one set of numbers. Quarter three: automation and better team mix. Quarter four: train leads to run it without me.

The result? At Hornbill, delivery got about 30% faster, and we could prove it.

So for me, without a starting number, you can't show improvement.

Likely follow-up: "What would you show leadership at the end of Q1?"

The starting numbers, the top three problems, the quick wins, and the yearly targets.

Likely follow-up: "What steps do you take to improve delivery efficiency and reduce operational cost without compromising quality?"

I measure first, remove waste, and check quality. At Hornbill, delivery got 30% faster. At Deluxe, productivity went up 20%.

q: Your organisation has 50+ Agile delivery teams, multiple vendors and distributed stakeholders, but delivery predictability is declining due to scope changes, dependency bottlenecks, technical debt and inconsistent Agile practices. How would you establish an enterprise delivery governance framework while maintaining team autonomy and improving predictability?
a:
With 50 teams, the problem is between the teams. So I add a few common rules, and let teams work freely inside them.

To be honest, my biggest setup was X teams. But I faced the same problems at NeuSix.

Here's what I would do. First, changes only come in at quarterly planning. Second, one board showing all dependencies and owners. Third, 15 to 20% of time for technical debt. And vendors follow the same rules.

The result? At NeuSix, a weekly dependency review made the biggest difference.

So for me, manage the links between teams, not the teams themselves.

Likely follow-up: "Isn't SAFe too heavy?"

It can be. I only use the parts we need, like joint planning.

q: Explain the architecture of a project you delivered.
a:
The Philips X-ray digital twin had five layers, from the hospital machine to the engineer's screen.

Here are the layers. First, the X-ray machines, which create data. Second, a secure gateway sends the data to the cloud, and removes personal details. Third, the data is cleaned and stored. Fourth, the digital twin and AI predict failures. Fifth, a dashboard shows the service team which machine needs a visit.

Everything was encrypted, because it was hospital data.

My job was to make sure the layers worked together, and the data could be trusted.

So for me, the hard part was never the AI. It was getting clean data.

Likely follow-up: "Why cloud and not on-premise?"

Each hospital is different. The cloud let us train one model for all machines.

q: How would you create an architecture for a new project?
a:
I never start from technology. I start from the business goal.

Here's how. First, agree the goal and what the system must do. Second, write down needs like users, speed, security and budget. Third, look at what already exists. Fourth, design in layers with my architects. Fifth, compare options and write the decision down. Sixth, test the riskiest part first, like we did for WIN Semiconductors.

For example, on Philips, this gave us a five-layer design (see question 62).

So for me, good architecture is one the client can afford, build and change.

Likely follow-up: "What if the client's architect disagrees?"

I compare the options against the needs and costs. The owner decides, and we write it down.

topic: Engineering Programs, Agile and Release Management
q: Tell me about your process for translating a product roadmap into engineering milestones and measurable release KPIs.
a:
I start from the result we want, then work back to releases and milestones.

Here's how. First, agree with Product which number each roadmap item should move. Second, break it into releases, riskiest first. Third, set milestones with dates and owners. Fourth, track two kinds of numbers: did we ship it, and did it work?

For example, on Philips, one goal became three stages, each with its own success measure.

So for me, a milestone says we shipped. A result says it mattered.

Likely follow-up: "What if Product keeps changing the roadmap?"

Change is fine, but we show what moves out when something comes in.

topic: Engineering Programs, Agile and Release Management
q: Describe a time you mediated technical architecture trade-offs between engineering teams without writing code yourself.
a:
I don't need to pick the technical answer. My job is to make the choice clear, and get a decision.

Let me give you an example. On Philips, the AI team wanted lots of machine data, often. The data team worried about hardware limits and cost.

Here's what I did. First, each lead wrote their option on one page: cost, risk and time. Second, we compared both options with the project goal. Third, Philips engineers joined, and we wrote the decision into the data agreement.

The result? The argument ended in one meeting.

So for me, compare options against the goal, not against each other.

Likely follow-up: "What if the teams still can't agree?"

I take both options to the technical owner, with my recommendation and a decision date.

topic: Engineering Programs, Agile and Release Management
q: How do you design a structured customer feedback intake process that feeds product prioritisation?
a:
Feedback should go into one list, get ranked, and change what we build. And customers should hear back.

Here's how. First, collect feedback in one place: tickets, meetings and interviews. Second, tag it the same way. Third, group it into themes. Fourth, rank the themes every month with Product. Fifth, tell customers what we decided.

For example, on Zolvit, repeat tickets and feedback from lawyers went into one list, and our 10% improvement time went to the top items.

So for me, feedback only matters if it changes the plan.

Likely follow-up: "How do you stop the loudest customer dominating?"

We rank by how many customers it affects, not by who shouts.

topic: Engineering Programs, Agile and Release Management
q: Describe how you coordinate go-to-market readiness: release notes, enablement and documentation timing.
a:
Release notes, training and documents are part of the release plan, with their own dates.

Here's how. First, put them on the plan. Second, give each one an owner. Third, include them in the go-live checklist. Fourth, train sales and support before launch. Fifth, check support tickets after launch.

For example, on Vigilant, the event version, the demo and the message were planned together, and the client showed it live.

So for me, a feature isn't launched until sales and support can explain it.

Likely follow-up: "Engineering finishes late and there's no time for documentation?"

Then the feature waits for the next release. I won't launch something customers can't use.

topic: Engineering Programs, Agile and Release Management
q: How do you balance delivery speed with quality for AI/ML and GenAI programs, especially under tight timelines?
a:
Under time pressure, I cut scope, not testing.

Here's how. First, agree what "good enough" means before we start. Second, run the AI tests automatically on every change. Third, ship fewer features, fully tested. Fourth, a person checks sensitive answers. Fifth, watch accuracy and cost after launch.

For example, on Vigilant, we launched two features early, both fully tested. The rest came on the original date.

So for me, AI speed without testing is just risk.

Likely follow-up: "The model isn't hitting the target score and the deadline is close?"

I give the sponsor options: a smaller launch, a human check, or a new date. I never quietly lower the bar.

topic: Engineering Programs, Agile and Release Management
q: How do you act as the primary "unblocker" when engineering dependencies slip mid-sprint?
a:
I do two things: protect this sprint today, and fix the cause so it doesn't happen again.

Here's how. First, any blocker older than two days comes to me. Second, the team works on other tasks meanwhile. Third, I go to the owner of the blocker with a clear ask and a date. Fourth, I tell Product the same day. Fifth, we fix the cause at the retrospective.

For example, on Philips, we used sample data so the AI team could keep working while the real data was late.

So for me, unblocking is helping the right person decide today.

Likely follow-up: "What if the blocking team has different priorities?"

I go to their lead with the impact. If needed, I go to their common boss with options.

topic: Engineering Programs, Agile and Release Management
q: How do you drive a cross-team AI release from kickoff through deployment sequencing, unblocking dependencies quickly?
a:
I run it as one release with one plan.

Here's how. First, agree the goal and who owns each part. Second, agree the connections between teams early. Third, one plan with a weekly meeting. Fourth, the AI must pass its tests before go-live. Fifth, go live in steps, with a way to roll back.

For example, on PaySFT, agreeing the API contracts early let teams build at the same time.

So for me, the risk is in the handovers, so that's where I put control.

Likely follow-up: "How do you roll back an AI release?"

We keep the old model ready. A switch takes us back in minutes.

topic: Engineering Programs, Agile and Release Management
q: How do you ensure Engineering, Product and leadership stay aligned through steering syncs and status reporting?
a:
I keep everyone on the same facts, and use meetings for decisions.

Here's how. First, one dashboard and one risk list for everyone. Second, the right detail for each group: engineers weekly, leaders monthly. Third, clear rules for red, amber and green. Fourth, steering meetings only cover problems and decisions.

For example, at NeuSix, I run steering this way with CEO sponsors on five programs.

So for me, alignment is not more meetings. It's the same facts for everyone.

Likely follow-up: "What if leadership just wants a green report?"

I give them the honest report, with a plan. A late surprise hurts trust more.

topic: Engineering Programs, Agile and Release Management
q: What would your first 30 days look like to establish repeatable release processes and feedback loops?
a:
In 30 days, I learn how releases work today, fix the biggest pain, and agree a simple rhythm with the teams.

Here's the plan. Week one: talk to everyone and study the last few releases. Week two: measure where we are. Week three: agree a release calendar and checklist. Week four: set up feedback after every release.

For example, at Hornbill, measuring first is how I proved a 30% improvement.

So for me, a process sticks when the team helped build it.

Likely follow-up: "What if a release is due in your first week?"

I don't stop it. I join it, help, and learn from it.

topic: Engineering Programs, Agile and Release Management
q: Explain your release governance system: sprint ceremonies, release trains and code-freeze sequencing for quality delivery.
a:
I set a fixed release rhythm and clear checks, so quality is planned, not argued about.

Here's how. First, normal sprint meetings with clear goals. Second, a release train: a fixed date, and anything not ready waits for the next one. Third, freeze features, test, then freeze code. Fourth, a go-live checklist signed by each owner.

For example, at Jazeera Airport, a 22-point checklist helped us launch on the date.

So for me, the date stays fixed. Only the scope moves.

Likely follow-up: "What happens when someone wants to squeeze in a late feature?"

It goes on the next train, unless the sponsor accepts the risk in writing.

topic: Engineering Programs, Agile and Release Management
q: Which tools and tracking processes do you own to maintain an engineering execution backbone across teams?
a:
Everyone tracks work the same way, in one place.

Here's what I use. Jira for work. Confluence for documents and decisions. One risk list. One board for dependencies. And one dashboard for leaders.

For example, at NeuSix, this gave us one view of all programs, and cut report time by half.

So for me, it works when nobody needs extra status slides.

Likely follow-up: "How do you get teams to keep the data up to date?"

I make it useful for them: fewer meetings, and data used to help, not blame.

topic: Engineering Programs, Agile and Release Management
q: How do you balance delivery speed, technical debt and quality?
a:
Speed, quality and technical debt are not a choice. If you skip quality today, you are slow tomorrow.

Let me give you an example. On PaySFT, we had 45 days and half a team. Skipping tests was tempting. On Zolvit, support work could eat all our time.

Here's what I did. First, on PaySFT, we kept testing and cut scope instead. Second, on Zolvit, we kept 10% of time for fixing technical debt. Third, we used automatic tests, so quality didn't slow us down.

The result? PaySFT launched on time, and Zolvit stayed stable.

So for me, quality is what makes speed last.

Likely follow-up: "How do you convince the business to spend time on technical debt?"

I show what it already costs: repeat bugs and slow changes.

topic: Engineering Programs, Agile and Release Management
q: Several squads depend on one platform team. How do you improve flow?
a:
When many teams wait for one team, I make the queue visible and fair.

Let me give you an example. At NeuSix, five programs shared the same AI and cloud engineers. Everyone wanted them first.

Here's what I did. First, one visible queue for all requests. Second, one simple rule for priority. Third, teams asked early, with dates. And we agreed interfaces early, so teams could work at the same time.

The result? The daily fights stopped.

So for me, don't push harder. Make the queue clear and smaller.

Likely follow-up: "Would you add people to the platform team?"

Only after the queue is clear. Often the problem is priorities, not people.

topic: Engineering Programs, Agile and Release Management
q: A release is at risk due to integration failures. What is your recovery plan?
a:
First, I find what's failing. Then I fix the most important parts first.

Let me give you an example. On Philips, the real machine data didn't match what we built, and integration failed.

Here's what I did. First, both teams listed every failure, with an owner. Second, we signed a data agreement with Philips. Third, we tested together every week.

The result? We passed all three stages. And if a date can't move, I launch what's ready, like at Jazeera Airport.

So for me, plan integration from day one.

Likely follow-up: "How do you stop it happening again?"

Agree the formats at the start, and test together every sprint.

q: Value versus velocity: your teams consistently meet sprint commitments, yet business stakeholders report that delivery isn't generating the expected value. How would you identify and address the underlying problem?
a:
If the team is fast but the business is unhappy, we are building the wrong things.

Let me give you an example. At DP World, we were delivering, but the business saw no value.

Here's what I did. First, we talked to the real users. Second, every task had to link to a business problem. Third, leaders saw business results, not team speed.

The result? The program turned around, and we won four new projects.

So for me, speed shows we're busy. Results show we're useful.

Likely follow-up: "What if the product owner insists the backlog is right?"

I bring the usage data, and we look at it with the sponsor.

q: Leadership under pressure: a high-performing delivery lead repeatedly misses commitments and blames external dependencies. How would you investigate the issue, establish accountability and improve performance?
a:
I check the facts before I judge the person. Even if others cause delays, the lead must manage them.

Let me give you an example. At Cosmos-Maya, good leads kept missing dates and blaming others.

Here's what I did. First, I checked the facts. Most delays came from known risks nobody owned. Second, I talked to each lead privately, with facts, not blame. Third, every risk got a name and a date.

The result? The leads started owning their risks.

So for me, you can't control every dependency, but you can see it early.

Likely follow-up: "What if performance still doesn't improve?"

After fair support, I start a formal process with HR.

q: Governance transformation: you join an organisation where delivery governance involves excessive reporting, frequent status meetings and slow decision-making. What changes would you introduce without losing executive visibility or control?
a:
Governance should make decisions faster. Leaders want no surprises, not more reports.

Let me give you an example. At NeuSix, people made status reports by hand. At Discreet Arts, leaders heard about delays too late.

Here's what I did. First, one place for all data in Jira. Second, a dashboard that warns early. Third, short meetings only about problems and decisions.

The result? We saw delays two to three weeks earlier.

So for me, less reporting, faster decisions.

Likely follow-up: "How do you switch without leaders feeling they've lost control?"

I run the new dashboard next to the old report for a month. Then we switch.

q: Strategic leadership: your organisation must deliver a major transformation within six months, but resources are limited and priorities keep changing. How would you build a realistic delivery strategy, prioritise initiatives and ensure sustainable execution?
a:
With six months and few people, you can't do everything. So I choose a few big goals.

Let me give you an example. At Cosmos-Maya, I had six months, no extra budget, and changing priorities.

Here's what I did. First, I checked every project. Second, one staffing plan, and my best people on the most important work. Third, every change in priority became a clear decision.

The result? By day 90, delivery was predictable again.

So for me, the real plan is deciding what not to do.

Likely follow-up: "What if leadership keeps adding priorities?"

I show what the new item pushes out. The sponsor decides.

q: How do you handle disagreements between technical teams and business stakeholders about delivery priorities?
a:
I don't take sides. I make the trade-off clear, and agree a rule.

Let me give you an example. On Zolvit, the business wanted features, and the tech team wanted stability time.

Here's what I did. First, both sides explained their case. Second, we agreed a rule: fixed time for stability, and the rest for features. Third, the business chose the order of features.

The result? Planning stopped being a fight.

So for me, agree the rule before you argue.

Likely follow-up: "What if they still disagree on one item?"

I take both options to the sponsor, with my recommendation.

q: How do you measure team performance and ensure accountability across different project teams?
a:
I use the same few numbers for every team, and every task has an owner.
