Let me give you an example. At NeuSix, every lead reported in a different way.

Here's what I did. First, one simple scorecard for all teams. Second, speed and quality measured together. Third, I use numbers to coach, not to punish.

The result? I can now see a team slipping in days.

So for me, accountability is easy when everyone sees the same facts.

Likely follow-up: "How do you stop teams gaming the numbers?"

Speed is always paired with quality.

q: Can you describe how you would handle a major production issue immediately after a project release while ensuring minimal business disruption?
a:
First, get the service back. Then find the cause. And keep the business informed.

Let me give you an example. On Zolvit, a live legal platform, an outage is very serious. So we prepared before anything went wrong.

Here's what I do. First, before release, have a rollback plan and alerts ready. Second, in an incident, one person leads, and we roll back if that's fastest. Third, the sponsor hears from me within an hour, with updates every 30 minutes. Fourth, after it's fixed, a no-blame review.

The result? Zolvit stayed stable.

So for me, in an incident, fixing fast and talking clearly matter more than blame.

Likely follow-up: "Would you roll back or fix forward?"

Roll back first, unless a small, tested fix is faster.

q: How do you ensure that multiple projects are delivered on time and within budget while maintaining quality standards? (Similar to a follow-up in question 9)
a:
I run every project with the same simple system. So problems with time, money or quality show up early.

Let me give you an example. At NeuSix, I run five programs at the same time.

Here's how. First, the same meetings for every project: daily, weekly and monthly. Second, one risk list for all projects. Third, quality built in with tests from the start. And I step in when a project starts to slip.

The result? When PaySFT lost half its team, we caught it early and still delivered in 45 days.

So for me, a good system shows problems while they are still small.

Likely follow-up: "What do you keep for yourself, and what do you delegate?"

I keep clients, big risks and money decisions. The rest goes to the leads.

q: How do you plan capacity across feature delivery, support and improvement work? (Similar to question 10)
a:
I split the team's time on purpose, and protect it. Otherwise, improvement work never happens.

Let me give you an example. On Zolvit, support tickets could use up all our time.

Here's what I did. First, support always came first. Second, we kept about 10% of time for improvements. Third, we picked improvements that reduced support work.

The result? The service stayed stable, and the client still got improvements.

So for me, improvement needs its own time.

Likely follow-up: "What if the client won't pay for improvement time?"

I show what the problems already cost. The improvement usually pays for itself.

q: Delivery recovery: you take over a critical project that is already three months behind schedule. How would you recover delivery without compromising quality or team morale? (Similar to a follow-up in question 11)
a:
When a project is late, I don't push harder on a broken plan. I make the plan smaller and honest.

Let me give you an example. On PaySFT, we lost half the team, and the client escalated.

Here's what I did. First, I told the client honestly in week one. Second, I cut the plan to the must-haves. Third, I kept testing, and I looked after the team: clear plan, no endless overtime.

The result? 125 APIs and two apps in 45 days, and the team stayed.

So for me, a smaller, honest plan saves a late project.

Likely follow-up: "Would you add more people?"

Only as a last step. New people slow the team down at first.

q: How do you manage a situation where a project is falling behind schedule and the client is expecting delivery as planned? (Similar to a follow-up in question 12)
a:
I tell the client early, with facts and options. Clients accept a new plan. They don't accept surprises.

Let me give you an example. On PaySFT, we lost half the team, but the client still expected the original plan.

Here's what I did. First, I told them in writing in week one. Second, I split must-haves from nice-to-haves. Third, I gave them a ₹32 lakh option to deliver everything.

The result? We delivered in 45 days, and the client trusted us again.

So for me, a missed date is a trust problem first.

Likely follow-up: "What if the date really can't move?"

Then the scope moves. The must-haves go live on the date, and the rest comes later.

q: Multi-team dependency management: how would you manage delivery risks when multiple engineering teams, vendors and business units depend on one another, but none reports directly to you? (Similar to a follow-up in question 14)
a:
When teams don't report to me, I lead with one shared goal and one plan everyone can see.

Let me give you an example. On Philips, four teams depended on each other, and some were outside our company.

Here's what I did. First, one shared goal: less machine downtime. Second, one plan for all four teams. Third, written agreements instead of orders, like our data agreement with Philips.

The result? We passed all three stages on one plan.

So for me, when everyone sees the same plan, they hold themselves to it.

Likely follow-up: "What if a team still doesn't deliver?"

I go to that team's manager with the facts and the cost of the delay.

q: Executive stakeholder conflict: two senior stakeholders have conflicting priorities, and both consider their requirements business-critical. How would you align them and reach a decision? (Similar to a follow-up in question 15)
a:
When two leaders both say theirs is most important, I don't pick a winner. I put the facts side by side.

Let me give you an example. At NeuSix, PaySFT needed more people, but Zolvit, a live service, needed its team too.

Here's what I did. First, I found out what each side really needed. Second, I showed both options with the cost and risk. Third, I kept Zolvit's team, and gave PaySFT a ₹32 lakh option.

The result? PaySFT delivered in 45 days, and Zolvit was never affected.

So for me, priority comes from business value, not from rank.

Likely follow-up: "What if they still can't agree?"

I take both options to their common boss, with my recommendation.

q: How do you manage resource allocation when multiple projects require the same critical team members? (Similar to a follow-up in question 15)
a:
I protect live services first. For the rest, I use an agreed rule. I never quietly move people.

Let me give you an example. At NeuSix, PaySFT needed people, but Zolvit still needed its support team.

Here's what I did. First, I didn't touch Zolvit's team. Second, I re-planned PaySFT for the team it had. Third, I gave the client a ₹32 lakh option. And long term, I train people in more skills.

The result? Both projects were fine.

So for me, priority comes from value, not noise.

Likely follow-up: "What if two leaders both say their project comes first?"

I show both options with the cost of delay, and take it to their common boss.

q: A product launch date is fixed but the scope is uncertain. How do you manage it? (Similar to question 16)
a:
If the date can't move, the scope must move.

Let me give you an example. At Jazeera Airport, the launch date was fixed. Some camera feeds were blocked close to launch.

Here's what I did. First, a clear go-live checklist. Second, I suggested launching the ready zones live, and recorded video for the rest. Third, the sponsor agreed in writing.

The result? We launched on the date. The rest went live weeks later.

So for me, don't fight the date. Change what goes live.

Likely follow-up: "How do you decide what the must-haves are?"

With the sponsor, based on the goal of the launch. Everything else goes to phase two.

q: What approach do you follow to manage client expectations and maintain long-term client relationships? (Similar to a follow-up in question 18)
a:
Three things: clear expectations at the start, no surprises, and value beyond the contract.

Let me give you an example. At DP World, we worked with the operations team for a long time.

Here's what I did. First, we agreed what success looks like. Second, I shared bad news early, with options. Third, I set up a weekly slot for small requests, so favours didn't become hidden work.

The result? The relationship grew into four new projects.

So for me, keep the goodwill, but keep promises clear.

Likely follow-up: "How do you handle an unhappy client?"

I listen, own our part, and agree a short recovery plan. Trust comes back through results.

q: How do you manage scope changes when a client requests additional features during an ongoing project? (Similar to a follow-up in question 20)
a:
I never just say no, and I never do extra work for free. I give options and write the decision down.

Let me give you an example. At DP World, the client sent quick requests on WhatsApp.

Here's what I did. First, I checked the impact. Second, I gave options: swap, smaller version, or a paid change. Third, a weekly slot for quick changes.

The result? The client got their changes, and the weekend work stopped.

So for me, changes are normal. Unmanaged changes break projects.

Likely follow-up: "What if the client says it was always in scope?"

We check the agreed scope together. If it's unclear, we agree a fair split.

q: Commercial accountability: a project is delivering successfully from a technical perspective, but its costs are exceeding the approved budget. How would you manage financial performance while protecting business outcomes? (Similar to a follow-up in question 22)
a:
If a project works well but costs too much, I find where the money goes and fix that first.

Let me give you an example. At Deluxe, we met every deadline, but costs were 18% over plan.

Here's what I did. First, I found that 35% of effort was rework. Second, we added our own review before the studio. Third, we automated steps and billed every change.

The result? Productivity up 20%, and costs back within 5% of plan.

So for me, cutting quality to save money is the most expensive mistake.

Likely follow-up: "What if you still can't close the gap?"

I tell the sponsor early and give a clear choice: more budget, less scope, or more time.

q: Predictability and risk forecasting: which delivery metrics would you use to predict future outcomes rather than simply report historical performance? How would you turn those insights into executive-level decisions? (Similar to a follow-up in question 23)
a:
I want numbers that warn me before things go wrong, not after.

Let me give you an example. At Discreet Arts, leaders heard about delays too late.

Here's what I did. First, I measured before changing anything. Second, I watched early signs, like missed promises and growing scope. Third, I gave leaders a range of dates, with the decision I needed.

The result? We saw delays two to three weeks earlier.

So for me, looking ahead gives you time to fix things.

Likely follow-up: "If you could track only one number?"

What we promised versus what we delivered.

q: How do you improve predictability without converting Agile teams into Waterfall teams? (Similar to a follow-up in question 23)
a:
Predictability comes from small pieces of work and real data, not from big plans.

Let me give you an example. At Hornbill, dates kept slipping.

Here's what I did. First, I measured how long work really took. Second, we limited work in progress and made tasks smaller. Third, we tracked promises versus delivery every sprint.

The result? Delivery got about 30% faster.

So for me, measure the flow, don't add paperwork.

Likely follow-up: "How do you give leadership a date without a Waterfall plan?"

I give a likely range from real data, and update it every sprint.

q: How do you identify and manage delivery risks before they affect project outcomes? (Similar to a follow-up in question 24)
a:
I look for early warning signs. Every big risk has an owner and a trigger.

Let me give you an example. On Philips, we built on guesses about the data, and it didn't match.

Here's what I did. First, a data agreement on day one, on every project. Second, I watch early signs. Third, clear escalation times: 48 hours, then five days.

The result? At Discreet Arts, we saw delays two to three weeks earlier.

So for me, a trigger tells you when to act.

Likely follow-up: "Can you give an example of a trigger?"

"If the vendor isn't in testing by the 15th, we switch to the backup."

q: Vendor performance crisis: a strategic vendor fails to meet critical milestones, putting a major product launch at risk. How would you manage contractual obligations, recovery planning and stakeholder communication? (Similar to a follow-up in question 25)
a:
When a vendor misses dates, I protect the contract, push for recovery, and prepare a backup.

Let me give you an example. At Deluxe, vendor delays put studio deadlines at risk.

Here's what I did. First, I used the contract to settle arguments. Second, one recovery plan for all vendors. Third, the studio heard about risks from me first.

The result? We met every studio deadline.

So for me, use facts and a backup plan, never surprises.

Likely follow-up: "What if the vendor still can't recover?"

Then I use the contract and switch to the backup.

q: How do you measure AI in delivery? (Similar to question 28)
a:
I measure AI in four ways: is it accurate, is it used, what does it cost, and does it help the business?

Let me give you an example. I have delivered AI on Zolvit, Vigilant and Philips.

Here's what I measure. First, accuracy, with a test set. Second, how many people use it. Third, cost per task. Fourth, the business result, like hours saved.

The result? On Vigilant, agents went live only after passing the score, with accuracy above X%.

So for me, if you don't measure before, you can't prove anything after.

Likely follow-up: "Which of the four matters most to a CXO?"

The business result. But the other three explain why.

q: What steps do you take to improve delivery efficiency and reduce operational costs without compromising quality? (Similar to a follow-up in question 60)
a:
I measure first, then remove waste, and always check quality.

Let me give you two examples. At Hornbill, delivery was slow. At Deluxe, costs were 18% over plan.

Here's what I did. First, at Hornbill, one priority list and less work in progress. Second, at Deluxe, less rework with our own review. Third, automation of repeated steps.

The result? Hornbill was 30% faster. Deluxe was back within 5% of plan.

So for me, most cost is hidden in rework and waiting.

Likely follow-up: "Where do you look first?"

Rework and waiting time.

q: Can you take me through the technical architecture of one of your projects? (Similar to question 62)
a:
Let me use PaySFT, the real estate platform. We built 125 APIs and two mobile apps in 45 days.

Here are the layers. First, two mobile apps and a web portal. Second, a gateway that checks logins and sends requests to the right place. Third, the APIs, grouped by business area. Fourth, a database, a cache, search and file storage. Fifth, a message queue for slow tasks, like notifications.

Across all layers, we had automatic tests, security scans, encryption and monitoring.

My main focus was the API contracts. We agreed them first, so mobile and backend teams could build at the same time.

So for me, I don't write the code, but I know where the risk is.

Likely follow-up: "Why microservices and not a monolith?"

Separate services let small teams work at the same time. For a small app, I'd start simple.

q: How do you report Agile delivery status to non-Agile executives? (Similar to question 71)
a:
Executives don't need to learn Agile. I tell them dates, money, risks and decisions, on one page.

Let me give you an example. At NeuSix, my CEO sponsors don't want story points.

Here's what I do. First, I report milestones, not sprints. Second, I give a range of dates. Third, clear colour rules, and every red item comes with a decision.

The result? Steering meetings became short and useful.

So for me, speak the business language.

Likely follow-up: "What if an executive wants a fixed date for everything?"

A date for what's committed, and a range for the rest.

q: Value versus velocity: your teams consistently meet sprint commitments, yet business stakeholders report that delivery isn't generating the expected value. How would you identify and address the underlying problem? (Similar to question 78)
a:
If the team is fast but the business is unhappy, we are building the wrong things.

Let me give you an example. At DP World, we were delivering, but the business saw no value.

Here's what I did. First, we talked to the real users. Second, every task had to link to a business problem. Third, leaders saw business results, not team speed.

The result? The program turned around, and we won four new projects.

So for me, speed shows we're busy. Results show we're useful.

Likely follow-up: "What if the product owner says the backlog is right?"

I bring the usage data, and we look at it with the sponsor.

q: Leadership under pressure: a high-performing delivery lead repeatedly misses commitments and blames external dependencies. How would you investigate the issue, establish accountability and improve performance? (Similar to question 79)
a:
I check the facts before I judge the person. Even if others cause delays, the lead must manage them.

Let me give you an example. At Cosmos-Maya, good leads kept missing dates and blaming others.

Here's what I did. First, I checked the facts. Most delays came from known risks nobody owned. Second, I talked to each lead privately, with facts, not blame. Third, every risk got a name and a date.

The result? The leads started owning their risks.

So for me, you can't control every dependency, but you can see it early.

Likely follow-up: "What if they still don't improve?"

After fair support, I start a formal process with HR.

q: Governance transformation: you join an organisation where delivery governance involves excessive reporting, frequent status meetings and slow decision-making. What changes would you introduce without losing executive visibility or control? (Similar to question 80)
a:
Governance should make decisions faster. Leaders want no surprises, not more reports.

Let me give you an example. At NeuSix, people made status reports by hand. At Discreet Arts, leaders heard about delays too late.

Here's what I did. First, one place for all data in Jira. Second, a dashboard that warns early. Third, short meetings only about problems and decisions.

The result? We saw delays two to three weeks earlier.

So for me, less reporting, faster decisions.

Likely follow-up: "How do you make the change without leaders feeling they've lost control?"

I run the new dashboard next to the old report for a month. Then we switch.

q: Strategic leadership: your organisation must deliver a major transformation within six months, but resources are limited and priorities keep changing. How would you build a realistic delivery strategy, prioritise initiatives and ensure sustainable execution? (Similar to question 81)
a:
With six months and few people, you can't do everything. So I choose a few big goals.

Let me give you an example. At Cosmos-Maya, I had six months, no extra budget, and changing priorities.

Here's what I did. First, I checked every project. Second, one staffing plan, and my best people on the most important work. Third, every change in priority became a clear decision.

The result? By day 90, delivery was predictable again.

So for me, the real plan is deciding what not to do.

Likely follow-up: "What if leadership keeps adding priorities?"

I show what the new item pushes out. The sponsor decides.

q: How do you deliver a roadmap when product priorities change every month? (Similar to question 81)
a:
When priorities change every month, I keep the goals steady, and review the list once a month.

Let me give you an example. At Hornbill, requests came from everywhere.

Here's what I did. First, one priority list and one way in. Second, goals per quarter, details only for the next few weeks. Third, changes reviewed once a month. Anything new pushes something out.

The result? Delivery got about 30% faster.

So for me, handle change at a fixed time, through one door.

Likely follow-up: "What if a senior leader wants a change right now?"

I show what it pushes out. The sponsor decides, and we write it down.

q: How do you handle disagreements between technical teams and business stakeholders about delivery priorities? (Similar to question 82)
a:
I don't take sides. I make the trade-off clear, and agree a rule.

Let me give you an example. On Zolvit, the business wanted features, and the tech team wanted stability time.

Here's what I did. First, both sides explained their case. Second, we agreed a rule: fixed time for stability, and the rest for features. Third, the business chose the order of features.

The result? Planning stopped being a fight.

So for me, agree the rule before you argue.

Likely follow-up: "What if they still disagree on one item?"

I take both options to the sponsor, with my recommendation.

q: How do you measure team performance and ensure accountability across different project teams? (Similar to question 83)
a:
I use the same few numbers for every team, and every task has an owner.

Let me give you an example. At NeuSix, every lead reported in a different way.

Here's what I did. First, one simple scorecard for all teams. Second, speed and quality measured together. Third, I use numbers to coach, not to punish.

The result? I can now see a team slipping in days.

So for me, accountability is easy when everyone sees the same facts.

Likely follow-up: "How do you stop teams gaming the numbers?"

Speed is always paired with quality.

q: Can you describe how you would handle a major production issue immediately after a project release while ensuring minimal business disruption? (Similar to question 84)
a:
First, get the service back. Then find the cause. And keep the business informed.

Let me give you an example. On Zolvit, a live legal platform, an outage is very serious. So we prepared before anything went wrong.

Here's what I do. First, before release, have a rollback plan and alerts ready. Second, in an incident, one person leads, and we roll back if that's fastest. Third, the sponsor hears from me within an hour, with updates every 30 minutes. Fourth, after it's fixed, a no-blame review.

The result? Zolvit stayed stable.

So for me, in an incident, fixing fast and talking clearly matter more than blame.

Likely follow-up: "Would you roll back or fix forward?"

Roll back first, unless a small, tested fix is faster.
